blocks.text: The fourth of those five fish is the אכספטיאם (Chulin 66b). The א is prosthetic, and כספטיאם appears to be the Greek Ξιφίας [Xiphias], in which case the ט must be elided; if, however, we drop the כ, then ספטיאם corresponds to the French Espadon and the Italian Spada, by which the swordfish is likewise designated. Buxdorf (Lex. p: 1068) also conjectures the Ξιφίας [Xiphias] in our word, and if we add that in the swordfish the dorsal fin gradually wears away, so that the originally undivided fin thereby appears as two fins, this corresponds in part to the Talmudic statement that the אכספטיאם is clean, because its fins and scales are lost over time.
חילק (A. Sara 39a; Halec, or Alec), סולתנית (ibid.) and, according to Rashi, also צחנתא (ibid.). In Aristotle, Pliny and Aelian the herring is not yet mentioned.

In our Talmudic passage חילק and סולתנית are identified with each other, for which reason Rashi's explanation of סולתנית at Chulin 66a by טונינא, Thonine, is incorrect, since the herring forms a genus of its own, whereas the tunny (אטונום, §. 317) is in that passage directly contrasted with the herring. [p. 260]
For the herring comes into the world with neither scales nor fins and acquires them only later, whereas the tunny has them early and only loses them later.

Now although the herring may be eaten, one should nevertheless not buy it from a heathen, because when it is caught the unclean fish ערבונה comes up with it and can easily be taken for it (A. Sara 39a); cf. the following §.

It should be noted, however, that later decisors did not understand חילק as the herring; thus Karo on Tur Jore Dea §. 83 cites authors who flatly assert that the herring (הרנגיש) is never salted together with unclean fish; since the Talmud expressly states that the חילק is customarily salted with unclean fish, those authors do not consider the חילק to be the herring. However, apart from the fact that the name seems all too closely related to the Latin Halec, that assertion about the admixture of foreign fish is also not yet to be accepted as unconditionally correct; cf. the following article. On the food of the whales, which consists chiefly of herrings (הרינגן), and which are sometimes still found inside the whale, cf. §. 180 and below §. 336.

A. Sara 39b it is ordained that one may not buy salted herrings from heathens, because together with the herring the unclean fish ערבונה is caught and salted and can therefore easily be confused with it; but one may buy the herrings from someone knowledgeable about fish, because he separates out the ערבונה (ibid. 34b). Here Rashi states that the ערבונה has a bad taste, spoils the herrings and may even be harmful to the whole load of the latter.

As regards first the name, it is taken not as a proper name but as a Nom. appellativ. from ערב "mixed," and the question arises which fish is to be thought of here as the admixture to the herrings. I conjecture the sprat (Clupea Sprattus); it is smaller than the herring, but likewise occurs in the North Sea and the Mediterranean, is salted like the herring and eaten as a finer kind of herring (Voigt l. c. 3, p. 248); some naturalists even take it to be the young herring, though erroneously, on which [p. 261] one may compare Blumenbach: Handbuch d. Naturg. p. 301. The fish expert will therefore sort out the sprat not as an inferior fish (as Rashi would have it) but as a better fish, by which that Talmudic ordinance can be accounted for; that the sprat was regarded as an unclean fish, however, is easily explained, since it has a pointed head (Voigt loc. cit.), which, as is well known, is a sign of uncleanness (§. 24).

עפיאן (Chulin 66a, for which, however, more correctly אפיאן) and עפיץ (A. Sara 39a, for which, however, more correctly עפרץ). The Ἀφύη [Aphyē], or Ἀφρός [Aphros] (Arist. l. c. 6, 14, 2) is the anchovy; it bears its name because it was believed to have arisen without reproduction (α-φυη [a-phyē]) from foam (Ἀφρός [Aphros]); therefore the reading אפיאן is to be preferred, since the alpha privativum is encountered several times: thus the young of a bird that is not yet fledged is called אפרוח from א-פרוח; the indivisible unit אחד from א-חד; the earth, held according to ancient view to be immovable, ארץ from א-רץ; cf. on this my contribution in the "Lien d'Israél" 1. année p. 126.
Of the anchovy the Talmud says (l. c.) that, like the herring, it comes into the world with neither scales nor fins, but acquires them later and is therefore clean.

מוניני. This word otherwise also means juice, thus מוניני דקמצי, the locust juice obtained by salting (Sabbat 110b), מוניני דנקירי, the juice of salted birds; but the word also occurs on its own and is rendered each time by Rashi as "small fish." Thus it is said: If a pregnant woman accustoms herself to eating מוניני, the children get trembling eyes (Ketuboth 60b). Eating מוניני is harmful after fasting (A. Sara 29a); finally it is related that Joab supplied the poor of the city with everything, even with מוניני and צנונא (§. 333), to which Rashi adds: These kinds of fish are delicate and true delicacies (Sanhedrin 49a). The word appears to be composed of מו "water" and נינו "fish"; specifically I conjecture the minnow (Cyprinus [p. 262] Phoxinus, engl. the Minow, Voigt (l. c. 3, p. 229) says of it: A small, tasty fish reaching only a few inches.
Only at Gittin 69b does Rashi translate the word by: צ׳ר דגים קטנים.
